newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ dlr rises, rates fall to keep conditions static.
newsitem.headline: NZ dlr rises, rates fall to keep conditions static.

text.p: The New Zealand dollar climbed back above 69 U.S. cents at the open on Friday in an apparent contradiction of this week's easing in monetary conditions.
But dealers said several large orders had bound the Kiwi temporarily to the newly-buouyant Australian currency, which was dragging it higher.
"There's a couple of large orders around to buy Kiwi and sell Aussie," said a chief bank dealer.

"So what's going to happen probably for the next day or so is you'll see Kiwi actually move in tandem with the Aussie, because people are trying to protect these orders and stop them getting triggered."
At Friday midday, the Kiwi was trading at US$0.6902/09 and at 68.64 on its Trade-Weighted Index, up from 0.6878/85 and 68.46 at Thursday's close.
On Tuesday, lower-than-expected March quarter inflation data sparked an easing in monetary conditions, with 90-day interest rates falling 17 basis points and the currency shedding 20 points.
Dealers said the Kiwi's strength on Friday, particularly in its Trade-Weighted Index, was helping rates to fall further but keeping the overall level of monetary conditions static.
"If Kiwi keeps moving up with the Aussie, the TWI will keep moving higher and our interest rates will keep moving lower again," the chief dealer said.
However, he said lower rates made the Kiwi less attractive to hold, which would eventually become an issue for the currency.
"It's becoming less and less attractive to hold Kiwi because you're just not picking up the returns.
"You've got higher interest rates in the United States and lower interest rates here, so the gap between U.S. interest rates and our interest rates has narrowed very considerably," he said.
"It will get to the point where the Kiwi will fall off quite markedly, but that could be a few weeks away."
